summary:
Burdur Province stands under Türkiye's national legal and policing framework, which leaves no separate provincial regime for a visitor to rely on. The Turkish Criminal Code and the national police powers that accompany it apply in full within the province, and the risks described below are national in scope rather than local quirks of Burdur.

The most consequential pending measure is the leaked 11th Judicial Package, described by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. The draft would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', with penalties of up to three years in prison, and would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years. It would also raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and require proof of permanent infertility, and would punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch calls the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The package had not been adopted when reported.

The gap between draft text and enforcement practice is the operational risk for a trans visitor. In 2025 police in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul stopped roughly twenty trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release. No fines were issued, but the women were documented. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee stated that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her. Foreign nationals stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk wherever appearance and passport gender marker diverge.

Hostility has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL report 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy', launched by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, documents anti-LGBTI+ hostility becoming institutionalised: senior officials' hate speech, instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The same organisation's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 a trans woman was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Carrying documents is itself a checkpoint risk. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Prison conditions matter for any trans visitor who is detained. Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, binary and heteronormative administration with no policy or staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints mechanisms that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern documented for 2025 is not new. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

The draft package's care provisions sit alongside the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, so the pressure on transition-related care comes from two directions at once: a pending statutory age floor of 25 with a permanent infertility condition, and an administrative reporting change that removes the 'other' option from hospital records. Neither is confined to a single province.

Enforcement already outpaces legislation. The GBT stops in Istanbul and the documentation of trans women without fines show that authorities are applying the substance of measures that remain in draft, which means a visitor should assess current police behaviour rather than the status of the bill.

Restrictions on expression and artistic freedom documented by Kaos GL affect public visibility generally, including any visible display of LGBT identity, and are enforced through regulatory and supervisory bodies rather than through the criminal courts alone.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same national framework, but the burdens fall differently on them than on visitors. Kaos GL's reporting is domestic and its 2025 findings were presented at a public launch by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, so the documentation of violations, detentions and hate speech is produced and contested inside the country.

Instructions issued to public institutions under the 'Year of the Family' banner shape how schools, registries and municipal offices treat LGBT residents, and regulatory and supervisory bodies restrict expression and artistic freedom for people who live and work here.

Residents held in custody are placed by registered sex, and the Sincan Women's Prison death of 1 December 2025 prompted coordinated demands for an independent investigation from Human Rights Association branches in six cities, with the matter raised in parliament on 12 December 2025 by opposition MP Sevda Karaca.

Access to transition-related care is governed by the Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 and by provincial health directorate circulars such as the one issued in Kayseri, which added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports. The removal of the 'other' option from hospital records affects residents' medical documentation directly.

Domestic opposition to the draft package is organised: 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have opposed the 11th Judicial Package, and the Prison Insider profile was prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of the 29 October 2025 reporting and had not been adopted at that point. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in the sources available here.

No source in this inventory records enforcement activity, GBT stops, detentions or violence specifically within Burdur Province. The province-level picture is inferred from the national framework and from incidents documented in Istanbul, Ankara and Kayseri; Burdur-specific policing data is not sourced.

The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 is described at national level. Its application to particular facilities in Burdur, and any provincial circular equivalent to the Kayseri one, is not sourced.

The 3,000 Turkish lira fine for failing to carry original identification and the associated detention warnings are stated as national rules; whether they have been applied in Burdur is not sourced.

The Human Rights Watch 2008 report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is offered as historical evidence only, not as a statement of current law.

The claim that GBT checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights is attributed to legal experts cited in the reporting; no court ruling establishing that position is included in the inventory.
